opus-5.5.text:
I think verification is really the hidden bottleneck, and honestly the hidden opportunity, in AI for Science.

If you look at where AI has made the most dramatic progress, it's almost always in domains where you can check the answer cheaply and reliably. Go has a clear win or loss. Code either passes the tests or it doesn't. In math, a formal proof checker like Lean tells you with certainty whether a proof is correct. That tight feedback loop is what lets you scale up search and reinforcement learning, because the model can try millions of things and get an honest signal back each time.

Science is messier. If an AI proposes a new material, a drug candidate, or a hypothesis about a biological pathway, the ground truth usually sits in a wet lab or a synthesis run, and that can take weeks or months and cost real money. So the speed of verification, not the speed of generation, ends up setting the pace of discovery. We can now generate candidates far faster than we can test them.

So I see progress coming along a few lines. First, building better intermediate verifiers: high-fidelity simulations, physics-based checks, learned surrogate models that are calibrated well enough to filter out the obviously bad ideas before anything touches a lab. Second, automating the experimental loop itself, with self-driving labs and robotic platforms that shrink the verification cycle from months to hours. Third, and I think this is underrated, being careful about what we count as "verified." A model can look great against a benchmark or a simulator and still be exploiting quirks of the checker rather than capturing real physics. Reward hacking isn't just a chatbot problem. It shows up in science too.

The fields that will move fastest are the ones that figure out how to turn their questions into something checkable, the way mathematics is doing with formalization. Where that's possible, I expect very rapid acceleration. Where verification stays slow and expensive, AI will still help a lot, but more as a prioritization tool that helps scientists decide which experiments are worth running, rather than something that discovers things on its own.

So for me, the core question for AI for Science isn't only "how smart is the model." It's "how fast and how honestly can we tell it when it's wrong."

r001.rationale: The response calls verification the “hidden bottleneck” in AI for Science and says its speed sets the pace of discovery.

r002.rationale: It links faster verification to tighter feedback loops, scaling search, and rapid acceleration, including shrinking experimental cycles from months to hours.

r003.rationale: The response discusses formal proof checking in mathematics but does not say mathematics has shifted from proof scarcity to proof oversupply.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think verification is really the bottleneck, more than idea generation. In my own field, condensed matter physics, it's actually not that hard to come up with a plausible hypothesis. What's hard is finding out whether it's true. You have to build the device, cool it down, run the measurement, and that cycle can take months.

So when people talk about AI accelerating science, I always ask: accelerating which part? A language model can now propose a hundred candidate materials or a hundred mechanisms in an afternoon. That's genuinely useful. But if each of those still takes a human team three months to check, you haven't sped up science very much. You've just moved the queue.

Where I think the real progress will come is in closing that loop. In some areas verification is cheap and rigorous, like mathematics, where you can run a proof through a formal checker, or code, where you can run the tests. Those areas will move very fast, and we're already seeing that. In experimental science the verification is physical, so the question becomes how much of it we can make automatic. Self-driving labs, robotic synthesis, high-throughput characterization, and better simulations that are trusted enough to stand in for an experiment. Each of those shrinks the loop.

There's a second meaning of verification too, which is epistemic. These models are very good at producing confident-sounding explanations, and a tired graduate student at two in the morning can be convinced by one. So the culture has to shift toward treating the model's output as a hypothesis, never as a result. The scientist's job becomes designing the cheapest experiment that can kill the idea. Honestly, that's what good scientists always did. AI just raises the stakes, because the supply of ideas is now effectively unlimited and the supply of careful checks is not.

If I had to summarize it: progress in AI for Science will be set by the rate at which we can verify, not the rate at which we can generate. The fields that figure out fast, trustworthy verification will pull ahead first.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls verification “the bottleneck” in AI for Science and says progress depends on the rate of verification.

r002.rationale: It says automating verification closes and shrinks the loop, and that fields with fast, trustworthy verification will move ahead. This communicates that overcoming the bottleneck enables faster scientific progress and iteration.

r003.rationale: The response says mathematical proofs can be checked cheaply and rigorously, but does not state that mathematics has shifted from proof scarcity to proof oversupply.

astra-6.text:
I think verification is central to progress in AI for Science, because producing a plausible answer is very different from establishing that it’s correct. A model can propose a molecule, a material, or an explanation for an observation—but we still need a reliable way to test that proposal.

The form of verification depends on the field. In mathematics, you may be able to check a proof formally. In physics, you can test consistency with known constraints, but ultimately you need agreement with experiment. In biology, even a very convincing computational prediction may require substantial experimental work.

So I would look beyond how many hypotheses an AI can generate and ask: how quickly can we close the loop between prediction, testing, and learning from the result? If generating candidates becomes cheap while experiments remain slow, verification becomes the bottleneck. Choosing the most informative experiment may then matter as much as generating the next hypothesis.

That’s where I see a major opportunity: AI helping us make claims that are precise enough to test, and helping us decide what to test next.

r001.rationale: It says verification becomes the bottleneck when AI generates candidates cheaply but experiments remain slow.

r002.rationale: It asks how quickly prediction, testing, and learning can be connected, but does not state that overcoming the bottleneck would enable rapid iteration.

r003.rationale: It discusses formal proof checking in mathematics, but does not describe a shift from proof scarcity to proof oversupply.

sol-6.1.text:
I think verification is one of the key things that will determine how far AI for Science can go. Generating a plausible hypothesis is becoming easier. Establishing that it’s correct—and understanding under what conditions it holds—is still hard.

In mathematics, you can sometimes verify a result with a formal proof. In physics, chemistry, or biology, you usually need experiments. A model can propose a new material, but you still have to make it and measure its properties. So progress depends partly on how quickly and reliably we can close that loop between prediction and experiment.

That also changes how we should evaluate these systems. A convincing explanation isn’t enough. We need testable predictions, reproducible results, and a clear account of uncertainty. If verification becomes faster and more accessible, AI can help us explore many more ideas while keeping scientific evidence at the center.

r001.rationale: The response says verification is still hard and will determine how far AI for Science can go, identifying it as a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It links faster verification and closing the prediction–experiment loop with exploring many more ideas, communicating faster iteration.

r003.rationale: It says mathematical results can sometimes be verified with formal proof, but does not describe a shift from proof scarcity to proof oversupply.
